limits: Python and libraries on this page: the examples run in your browser, in Python 3.13.2 with pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0 (the versions the research ran) on Pyodide's own lxml 6.0.0, Pillow 11.3.0 and cryptography 45.0.5, while the research ran under Python 3.14.6 with lxml 6.1.3, Pillow 12.3.0 and cryptography 50.0.2. Every example was run in the browser and compared with its stored result. The page's Chapter examples are the 28 code examples of the deck, taken from the deck's chapter-code manifest (same code, same order); each was run in the browser's Python (Pyodide 0.28.2) and its result compared with the manifest's recorded result before the page was built. Three examples were rewritten for research version 1.0.2 so that they give the same result there: DamagedInput (the pdfminer.six part is left to the description and pypdf's logged warning is silenced), ImagesNeedPillow (the modules it removes are put back) and WriteNeedsBinaryFile (pypdf's logged warning is silenced while it runs).

Recorded, not run: two examples need something a browser cannot give and show the output recorded under Python 3.14.6, labelled so: PdfminerAlternative, OptionalDependencyAes. pdfminer.six is not embedded (its wheel is 6.6 MB of character-map data); the second one starts a second Python in which the cryptography package is made unavailable.

The two libraries: pypdf (BSD-3-Clause), python_docx (MIT) are embedded as the PyPI wheels, unchanged, and unpacked in the browser; their licences are BSD-3-Clause and MIT (recorded in 03-materials/ch17/assets/ASSETS_PROVENANCE_v1_0_0.md). No file of the book's online materials (a zip of 7,759,877 bytes) is on the page: every example builds its own PDF and Word files, so there is no licence question about a shipped file.

NOT EXECUTED: Microsoft Word itself and any PDF viewer (LibreOffice 24.2 and the poppler and qpdf tools stood in for them), the language model clean-up of extracted text, the Mu editor, the book's figures as drawn, and the Practice Programs as readers would write them (the programs were written and run on files made for the purpose).

The PDF Password Breaker: its worst case (the book's dictionary of 349,900 words, both cases of each, 699,800 attempts, a password that is not in it) was run to the end on a file written by pypdf 6.20.1: 241.7 seconds for RC4, the default of encrypt(), and 1467.5 seconds for AES-256, the two started together on a machine with two cores. Each is one measured run on one machine and the page does not repeat it; the deck labels it so on slide 16.

What the public sites answered on 2026-10-12 is in live_observations_v1_0_0.json: the chapter's page (status 200, 100,057 bytes, equal to the digest in the book's ontology), the newest PyPI releases (pypdf 6.20.1, python-docx 1.2.0) and the pages of the stories. It is one request each, on one day, and nothing re-checks it.

One program was run under 10 interpreters (3.11.17, 3.12.3, 3.13.16, 3.14.0, 3.14.1, 3.14.2, 3.14.3, 3.14.4, 3.14.5, 3.14.6) with the same package versions; the items that differ between them are listed in interpreter_record_v1_0_0.json. The book's Appendix A pins pypdf 5.0.1 and python-docx 1.1.2, and the chapter's statements were also replayed with those; a result that names a version is a result for that version.

findings: Background

Chapter 17 of the 3rd edition, PDF and Word Documents, teaches PDF with the PyPDF package (extract text, post-process it with a language model, extract images, copy pages into a new file, rotate pages, insert blank pages, merge a watermark or overlay, encrypt and decrypt), Project 12 that combines select pages from many PDFs, and Word with the Python-Docx package (read paragraphs and runs, get the full text, style paragraphs and runs, apply run attributes, write paragraphs, headings, line and page breaks and pictures), and it ends with 12 practice questions and three practice programs, PDF Paranoia, Custom Invitations and PDF Password Breaker. The chapter page of 2026-10-12 is 100,057 bytes with 32 listings (19 of them interactive sessions of 91 statements), 10 captioned figures and 1 table, and its sha256, 00cb1643dca3afd3b75bfd9ce7ad594f3dd80f8606de1cffe40b8583846b4789, equals the chapterDigest of the book's own chapter ontology [P01] [P03] [P04].
Comparative analysis

The chapter's interactive sessions were replayed statement by statement, in order, on the files the book ships under Python 3.14.6 with pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0: of 91 statements 89 printed what the page prints and 2 differ, both in the same place, the third run of the demo paragraph, which the page prints as ' and some ' and which is ' text and some ' in the shipped demo.docx. Under the versions Appendix A pins, pypdf 5.0.1 and python-docx 1.1.2, 88 match and 3 differ: the same two and writer.merge(2, 'Recursion_Chapter1.pdf', (0, 5)), which raises AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'startswith'. The agreement is smaller than it looks: a statement that prints nothing cannot differ from the page, so the next finding concerns one that matches and still goes wrong [P01] [P02] [P05] [P06] [P19].
Comparative analysis

The chapter's merge() example, writer.merge(2, 'Recursion_Chapter1.pdf', (0, 5)), prints nothing and so matches the page under pypdf 6.20.1, but it does not do what the chapter says: the tuple lands in the third parameter, outline_item, so the library made a bookmark titled (0, 5) and inserted the whole 18-page file, and a writer of 5 pages ended with 23, identically on ten interpreters (3.11 to 3.14.6). With pages=(0, 5) the same call inserted 5 pages. append() accepts the tuple in its second place because the signature types its outline_item parameter as a title or a page range, and the signature of merge() types it as a title only. pypdf 5.0.1 raises AttributeError for the same line [P01] [P10] [P14] [P16].
Comparative analysis

Project 12 as printed does not run: the loop appends to pdf_files, a name never defined, and Python 3.14.6 answers NameError: name 'pdf_files' is not defined, suggesting pdf_filenames. The shipped combine_pdfs.py is not the finished program either: it stops at NameError: name 'PdfWriter' is not defined, because it writes PdfWriter without the pypdf prefix, and it also names pdf_files in its loop. With the name corrected the program combined three small files into combined.pdf of 5 pages (every page but the first of each), and a second run read combined.pdf as one of its own inputs and wrote 9 pages, which the program does not guard against. The test filename.endswith('.pdf') also misses a file named with capital letters [P01] [P02] [P35].
Comparative analysis

The book's two shipped scripts for text and images are the listings of the chapter, with Windows line endings: extractpdftext.py and extractpdfimages.py equal the printed text. Run on the shipped Recursion_Chapter1.pdf the text script wrote 32,981 characters in 688 lines and 5,363 words, with 11 warnings on the error stream that name fontTools, and the page texts are joined with no separator (page 1 ends with the words Al Sweigart and page 2 begins with 2 and Chapter 1, which run together as Al Sweigart2). The image script wrote 11 files of 2,099,648 bytes under the newest releases and 2,074,308 under the pinned ones, 7 images from page 1; the sample output the chapter prints says page 7 was skipped with not enough image data, and neither environment skipped it: both wrote 10_page7_Im0.tif. The zip does not hold encrypted.pdf, helloworld.docx or restyled.docx, which the chapter names as files the reader makes [P01] [P02] [P07] [P09].
Comparative analysis

Several statements about Word documents differ from the current package. The chapter prints a list of default style names (34 of them); a new document has 164 styles of four kinds (27 character, 1 list, 36 paragraph, 100 table), 'List Number ' with the trailing space the page prints raises KeyError, and MacroText is the id of a style named macro, which works only through a deprecated lookup by id that warns. A paragraph accepts only paragraph styles and a run only character styles: assigning 'Quote Char' to a paragraph or 'Quote' to a run raises ValueError. The paragraph list of a document does not include text in tables or headers, and text inside a hyperlink is in paragraph.text but in no run. The text script shipped as readDocx.py joins paragraphs with a blank line, so the output differs from the six lines the page prints [P01] [P02] [P20] [P21] [P22] [P24].
Comparative analysis

Table 17-1 lists twelve text attributes as attributes of a Run, and only three are: bold, italic and underline; strike, double_strike, all_caps, small_caps, shadow, outline, rtl, imprint and emboss exist on run.font. Assigning run.strike = True raises nothing and changes nothing (font.strike stayed None, no element in the XML), so the chapter's table sends a reader to a silent failure. The tri-state values are as the chapter says: None writes nothing, True writes <w:b/>, False writes <w:b w:val=0/>. The heading levels are given as 0 to 4 in one sentence and 1 to 9 in the next, and add_heading accepts 0 to 9 and raises ValueError outside it, which is also the answer to practice question 12 [P01] [P23] [P24].
Comparative analysis

Two optional dependencies and a default that the chapter does not mention matter in practice. page.images needs the Pillow package and raises ImportError without it. AES needs the cryptography package: without it AES-128 fails later, at write(), and AES-256 fails at encrypt(), both with DependencyError. encrypt() without an algorithm wrote RC4 with a 128-bit key (V 2, R 3), and algorithm='AES-256' wrote V 5, R 6 with qpdf reporting AESv3; the chapter shows only the AES-256 form. The chapter's text names neither Pillow nor cryptography, and the versions the book pins are given only in Appendix A, pypdf 5.0.1 and python-docx 1.1.2 [P01] [P05] [P09] [P11] [P13] [P41].
Comparative analysis

Text extraction is weaker than the chapter's tone suggests and the gap is documented: a PDF stores drawing commands, so the text comes out in stream order (worldHello for a page that shows Hello world), a black rectangle drawn over text leaves the text in the file, and a scanned page returned the empty string with one image. pypdf documents post-processing as outside its scope. On the sample chapter pdfminer.six returned 33,200 characters against pypdf's 32,981, put a form feed after every page and spaced out the chapter heading (W H A T), and of eleven damaged files none was read by pdfminer.six and refused by pypdf, so the fallback the chapter's listing offers was not needed in any of them [P07] [P08] [P27] [P40] [P44].
Comparative analysis

The first practice program, PDF Paranoia, takes its password from the command line, where any program that lists processes can read it (CWE-214), and deletes each original after a test decryption; written as the chapter asks, it encrypted the PDFs of a small folder tree with AES-256, removed the originals, skipped an already encrypted file, and decrypted with a wrong password without stopping. A filter on the lower-case extension .pdf misses C.PDF. The second practice program, Custom Invitations, needs styles that exist in the template; the study made them in code with styles.add_style, and a page break after every guest left no blank last page in LibreOffice 24.2, which counted 5 pages for 5 guests [P01] [P22] [P43] [P52].
Comparative analysis

The worst case of the PDF Password Breaker, run to the end on a file written by pypdf 6.20.1 with the book's dictionary.txt (349,900 words, both cases of each, so 699,800 attempts) and a password that is not in the list, found nothing and took 241.7 seconds for RC4, the default of encrypt(), and 1467.5 seconds for AES-256, the two runs started together on a machine with two cores. The page speaks of 88,000 attempts; the shipped file gives 699,800 (8.0 times the 44,000 words on the page), and a stronger algorithm costs about six times as much per guess, so the chapter's remark that a long random password defeats the program is shown by the timing, not only stated. Python 3.14.6.
Comparative analysis

One program that exercises both packages was run under ten interpreters installed with uv: 3.11.17, 3.12.3, 3.13.16 and the seven releases 3.14.0 to 3.14.6, with the same pypdf, python-docx and pdfminer.six. Eleven results were equal in all ten: the page count (18), the images per page, the hash of the text from pypdf and from pdfminer.six, every pypdf operation (append (0, 5) gave 5 pages, (0, 5, 2) gave 3, [0, 5] gave 2, merge with pages=(0, 2) gave 4, rotation 90, encrypted file V 5 R 6), the python-docx operations, the silent ignoring of run.strike, the warning for the style id and the 23 pages of the chapter's merge line. The only difference was the build of the cryptography wheel on 3.13 (50.0.1 against 50.0.2). The chapter's PDF and Word behaviour does not depend on the 3.x release [P06] [P19] [P27] [P50].
Comparative analysis

A PDF or Word file made by the chapter's listings opens elsewhere: LibreOffice 24.2 converted the seven Word files the study wrote (hello world, multiple paragraphs, headings, two pages, a picture, the restyled file and demo.docx) to PDF, counted 2 pages for the file with the page break and 1 for the others, and showed the text; qpdf --check accepted the PDF written by hand and by pypdf, and pdftotext without the password refused the encrypted file and read it with it. Microsoft Word itself, a PDF viewer and the language model clean-up of the section Post-Processing with AI were NOT EXECUTED, and the statement that the style names in the Styles pane of Word match the list the chapter prints is therefore checked only against the template of python-docx [P01] [P41] [P42] [P52].
Conclusion

For an advanced course, chapter 17 is best taught as a limit on what can be automated: a PDF is a page description made for display and a .docx is a zip of XML parts, so a program can copy, reorder, rotate, stamp, encrypt, read the paragraphs and runs of and write a new document, and cannot recover structure that was never stored. The sections to correct are few and exact: pass pages= to merge(), rename pdf_files in Project 12 and guard against reading its own output, take heading levels as 0 to 9, set run attributes through run.font, use the style names the template has (no trailing space, no MacroText), name Pillow and cryptography, and keep the password of PDF Paranoia out of the command line. The sections to add are the file formats themselves, redaction that does not remove text, scanned pages, and the size of a brute-force attack. The 91 statements, the 12 corpus programs and the 70 examples of this study are the evidence [P01] [P06] [P19] [P40] [P43] [P44].
Contemporary developments

The packages have moved on since the chapter's examples. The pypdf documentation tells that pyPdf (2005, Mathieu Fenniak) was forked as PyPDF2 at the end of 2011, that Martin Thoma took over PyPDF2 in April 2022 and that it was merged back into pypdf; PdfMerger, which older tutorials use, was removed in pypdf 5.0.0 (in 5.0.1 the name exists and raises DeprecationError, in 6.20.1 it is gone), and PdfFileReader and PdfFileWriter are not names of pypdf 6.20.1 either. Appendix A pins pypdf 5.0.1 and python-docx 1.1.2 while PyPI offers pypdf 6.20.1 and python-docx 1.2.0; an attempt to install Pillow 10.4.0 for the pinned environment found no wheel for Python 3.14 and the build failed for lack of libjpeg headers, so that environment used the newest Pillow. The package docx, which the chapter warns against, is at 0.2.4 from 6 February 2014 and its import fails under Python 3.14.6 with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'exceptions' [P05] [P16] [P17] [P28] [P29] [P30].

nodes.label: Pdf format
nodes.body: The chapter opens by saying that PDF and Word are binary files that also hold font, colour and layout information, so a program cannot simply pass their filenames to open(), and that a PDF is great for laying out text for people to print and read and is not easy to parse into plaintext (Sweigart, 2025). The PDF standard describes the file as a header, numbered objects, a cross-reference table and a trailer, and the text of a page as drawing commands (Adobe Systems, 2008)(Library of Congress, 2019).

paras.text: The chapter opens by saying that PDF and Word are binary files that also hold font, colour and layout information, so a program cannot simply pass their filenames to open(), and that a PDF is great for laying out text for people to print and read and is not easy to parse into plaintext (Sweigart, 2025). The PDF standard describes the file as a header, numbered objects, a cross-reference table and a trailer, and the text of a page as drawing commands (Adobe Systems, 2008)(Library of Congress, 2019).

Two ideas carry this subject. File structure covers the header and trailer, the cross-reference table, the content stream and the producer metadata. Text and layout covers why text comes out in stream order, why a scanned page has none, why a black box does not redact and why a PDF has no paragraphs. A small PDF written by hand for each example makes every number below reproducible (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: File structure
nodes.body: A PDF file starts with a header line that names the version, is followed by numbered objects, and ends with a cross-reference table, a trailer and the line %%EOF; the pages, the fonts and the drawing commands of each page are such objects (Adobe Systems, 2008)(Library of Congress, 2019). The chapter does not describe the file, only the PyPDF objects that stand for it (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A PDF file starts with a header line that names the version, is followed by numbered objects, and ends with a cross-reference table, a trailer and the line %%EOF; the pages, the fonts and the drawing commands of each page are such objects (Adobe Systems, 2008)(Library of Congress, 2019). The chapter does not describe the file, only the PyPDF objects that stand for it (Sweigart, 2025).

A two-page file was written byte by byte and read back to show the four parts: the header and trailer, the table of offsets, the content stream of a page and the producer entry a library leaves. The same file passed qpdf --check and was read by pypdf and pdftotext (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Header and trailer
nodes.body: A PDF file begins with a header line such as %PDF-1.4 and ends with the keyword startxref, the byte offset of the cross-reference table and the marker %%EOF; the standard says a reader finds the table by reading from the end of the file (Adobe Systems, 2008)(Library of Congress, 2019). The chapter never opens a PDF as bytes, since PyPDF does it (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A PDF file begins with a header line such as %PDF-1.4 and ends with the keyword startxref, the byte offset of the cross-reference table and the marker %%EOF; the standard says a reader finds the table by reading from the end of the file (Adobe Systems, 2008)(Library of Congress, 2019). The chapter never opens a PDF as bytes, since PyPDF does it (Sweigart, 2025).

A two-page file written for the study began with %PDF-1.4, ended with %%EOF, and its startxref offset pointed at the bytes xref. The file passed qpdf --check and pypdf read two pages from it (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: A PDF file starts with a header line, here %PDF-1.4, and ends with the word startxref, a byte offset and %%EOF; in a two-page file written for the study the offset pointed at the bytes xref and the last line was %%EOF, so a reader finds the table by reading from the end.

nodes.label: Cross reference table
nodes.body: The cross-reference table lists, for each numbered object of the file, the byte offset at which the object starts and whether it is in use; entry 0 is the head of the list of free objects (Adobe Systems, 2008). A reader that has the table can jump to any page without reading the whole file (Library of Congress, 2019).

paras.text: The cross-reference table lists, for each numbered object of the file, the byte offset at which the object starts and whether it is in use; entry 0 is the head of the list of free objects (Adobe Systems, 2008). A reader that has the table can jump to any page without reading the whole file (Library of Congress, 2019).

The table of the two-page file had 8 entries, the first free, and the offsets of entries 1 to 3 pointed at the text 1 0 obj, 2 0 obj and 3 0 obj. That is why a file cut off before its table cannot be opened, as the damaged-input leaf shows (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: The cross-reference table lists the byte offset of every numbered object: the table of the two-page file had 8 entries, the first (object 0) free, and the offsets of the first three used entries pointed at the text 1 0 obj, 2 0 obj and 3 0 obj.

nodes.label: Content stream text
nodes.body: The chapter extracts the text of a page with extract_text(), and the PDF standard says the text of a page is a content stream of drawing commands: BT begins a text object, Tf selects a font and size, Td moves to a position, Tj shows a string and ET ends it (Sweigart, 2025)(Adobe Systems, 2008).

paras.text: The chapter extracts the text of a page with extract_text(), and the PDF standard says the text of a page is a content stream of drawing commands: BT begins a text object, Tf selects a font and size, Td moves to a position, Tj shows a string and ET ends it (Sweigart, 2025)(Adobe Systems, 2008).

For the page of the study the stream was BT /F1 18 Tf 72 720 Td (Page one) Tj ET, and get_contents().get_data() returned those bytes exactly. The words are placed at coordinates and nothing in the stream says that they form a sentence or a paragraph (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Producer metadata
nodes.body: A PDF may carry document information such as the producer and creation date; the chapter does not read metadata, and the pypdf documentation says the reader's metadata attribute gives it (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). A file that a library writes records the library as its producer.

paras.text: A PDF may carry document information such as the producer and creation date; the chapter does not read metadata, and the pypdf documentation says the reader's metadata attribute gives it (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). A file that a library writes records the library as its producer.

The file written by hand had no metadata (None). After pypdf appended its page to a PdfWriter and wrote the result, the metadata held only the producer, pypdf. The shipped sample chapter says Adobe PDF Library 16.0.5, and the first_five_pages.pdf the chapter writes says pypdf (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: A hand-made file had no metadata (None); after pypdf copied it into a PdfWriter and wrote it, the document information held {'/Producer': 'pypdf'}, so a file saved by the library names the library as its producer.

nodes.label: Text and layout
nodes.body: The chapter warns that PDFs are great for laying out text for people and are not easy to parse into plaintext, and lists the choices that extraction cannot make by itself: where paragraphs end and begin, whether page numbers, headers and footers are included, how tables are converted and how much whitespace is kept (Sweigart, 2025). The PDF standard places text with drawing commands at coordinates, in the order the stream gives them (Adobe Systems, 2008).

paras.text: The chapter warns that PDFs are great for laying out text for people and are not easy to parse into plaintext, and lists the choices that extraction cannot make by itself: where paragraphs end and begin, whether page numbers, headers and footers are included, how tables are converted and how much whitespace is kept (Sweigart, 2025). The PDF standard places text with drawing commands at coordinates, in the order the stream gives them (Adobe Systems, 2008).

Small pages with known drawing commands show what follows: the text comes out in stream order, a page that is only a picture has no text, a black rectangle drawn over text does not remove it, and separate drawing commands extract as separate lines (This study, 2026).

The standard lets a page draw its strings in any order, because each Td or Tm command says where the next string goes (Adobe Systems, 2008).

nodes.label: No paragraphs in pdf
nodes.body: The chapter asks where paragraphs in the PDF should end and begin, and answers that these are subjective decisions of the extraction (Sweigart, 2025). A PDF stores each string where it is drawn, so a paragraph exists only as a group of lines that a human sees (Adobe Systems, 2008).

nodes.label: Pdf text and images
nodes.body: The first task of the PDF section is to read a PDF with PyPDF: open a PdfReader, loop over its pages, call extract_text() on each and add the strings together, then write the text to a file, with pdfminer.six as a fallback when PyPDF cannot open a file, and extract the images of each page and write them to files (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). The chapter says PyPDF might make mistakes when extracting text and may fail to open some PDFs, and that cleaning the extracted text is boring and cannot easily be automated (Sweigart, 2025).

Each was run on small files and the chapter's loops on the shipped sample chapter (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Joined pages no separator
nodes.body: The chapter's extraction listing sets text to an empty string and, for each page, adds the text of the page with +=, then writes the result to a file (Sweigart, 2025). extract_text() returns the text of one page without a trailing newline or a page marker (pypdf contributors, 2026).

Six pages gave Page 1Page 2Page 3Page 4Page 5Page 6. On the shipped chapter the end of page 1, Al Sweigart, and the start of page 2, 2 and Chapter 1, ran together as Al Sweigart2. A program that wants page boundaries must join the texts with a separator of its own (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Adding each page's text to one string with += joins the pages with nothing between them, giving Page 1Page 2Page 3Page 4Page 5Page 6, and the last word of a page runs into the first of the next; joining with a newline keeps them apart.

nodes.body: The chapter says PyPDF can make mistakes, offers the pdfminer.six function extract_text() as a fallback for a file PyPDF cannot understand, and suggests a language model prompt to clean up hyphens, headers and paragraph breaks (Sweigart, 2025)(pdfminer.six contributors, 2026). The pypdf documentation lists extraction modes and says post-processing is outside the library (pypdf contributors, 2026).

The pypdf documentation lists extraction modes and says post-processing is outside the library (pypdf contributors, 2026).

The same page was extracted in the default and in the layout mode, the same six-page file went through pdfminer.six, damaged files went through both libraries, and a hyphenated row was repaired by a regular expression. The language model clean-up was NOT EXECUTED (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Layout mode
nodes.body: The chapter calls extract_text() with no argument. The pypdf documentation shows extraction_mode='layout', which extracts text in a fixed-width format that closely adheres to the rendered layout of the source PDF (pypdf contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter calls extract_text() with no argument. The pypdf documentation shows extraction_mode='layout', which extracts text in a fixed-width format that closely adheres to the rendered layout of the source PDF (pypdf contributors, 2026).

A page with Name and Price on one row and Tea and 3 on the next gave Name Price and Tea 3 by default, and in the layout mode the gap between the columns was kept as runs of spaces, so the numbers stand under their headings. The chapter does not mention the mode (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: The default extraction joins the words of a row with single spaces (Name Price and Tea 3), and extraction_mode='layout' keeps the horizontal gap between columns with runs of spaces, so a table-like page can be read column by column.

nodes.body: When PyPDF cannot understand an unconventional file the chapter turns to pdfminer.high_level, whose extract_text() function takes the filename and returns the whole text as one string, written to a file (Sweigart, 2025)(pdfminer.six contributors, 2026).

nodes.label: Damaged input
nodes.body: The chapter says PyPDF may fail to open some PDFs and that the author has not met one it could not open (Sweigart, 2025). The fallback it offers is pdfminer.six (Sweigart, 2025)(pdfminer.six contributors, 2026).

A six-page file cut off before its cross-reference table raised PdfStreamError in pypdf and PDFSyntaxError in pdfminer.six; an empty file raised EmptyFileError in pypdf. nodes.label: Pdf writing
nodes.body: The second task is to create a new PDF from pages of existing ones: a PdfWriter starts empty, copies pages from files with append() and merge(), rotates them, adds blank pages, merges a watermark or overlay and encrypts the result, and PdfReader decrypts a protected file (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). Project 12 puts the copying to work by combining the pages after the first of every PDF in a folder into one file (Sweigart, 2025).

Five ideas carry this subject. Page selection covers the tuple, the step and the list of pages. Insert and merge covers merge() at a position, the positional tuple trap and the size of a blank page. Page editing covers rotation, the watermark and the overlay. Protection covers the two algorithms, the return values of decrypt() and the empty user password. API history covers the names that older tutorials use. Each was run on pypdf 6.20.1 (This study, 2026).

The write() method saves the writer to a file opened in binary write mode (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Merge positional tuple trap
nodes.body: The chapter prints writer.merge(2, 'Recursion_Chapter1.pdf', (0, 5)) with the tuple as the third positional argument and shows no output (Sweigart, 2025). The signature of merge() in pypdf 6.20.1 is position, fileobj, outline_item, pages (pypdf contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter prints writer.merge(2, 'Recursion_Chapter1.pdf', (0, 5)) with the tuple as the third positional argument and shows no output (Sweigart, 2025). The signature of merge() in pypdf 6.20.1 is position, fileobj, outline_item, pages (pypdf contributors, 2026).

The tuple went to outline_item: the writer got a bookmark titled (0, 2) and the whole six-page file, 9 pages in all instead of 5; in the shipped chapter case 23 pages instead of 10. pypdf 5.0.1 raised AttributeError, tuple has no attribute startswith. The call must be written with pages= The tuple that works is the one of Append range tuple, passed as pages. (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Written as the chapter writes it, merge(1, file, (0, 2)), the tuple lands in the parameter outline_item and not in pages: pypdf 6.20.1 made a bookmark titled (0, 2) and inserted the whole six-page file, so the writer ended with 9 pages and not 5; the parameters are self, position, fileobj, outline_item and pages, and pypdf 5.0.1 raises AttributeError instead.

nodes.label: Blank page size
nodes.body: The chapter says that the size of a new blank page will be the same as that of the preceding page, and creates one with add_blank_page() at the end and one with insert_blank_page(index=2) (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says that the size of a new blank page will be the same as that of the preceding page, and creates one with add_blank_page() at the end and one with insert_blank_page(index=2) (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

At the end add_blank_page() took the size of the last page. For the inserted page the size came from the page that follows it: between a 300 by 400 page and a 100 by 100 page the new page was 100 by 100. A blank page in an empty writer raised PageSizeNotDefinedError (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: A new blank page takes its size from a page already in the writer: add_blank_page() after a 200 by 200 page made another 200 by 200 page, and insert_blank_page(index=1) between a 300 by 400 page and a 100 by 100 page took 100 by 100, the size of the page that follows it, and not the 300 by 400 of the page before it that the chapter's words suggest.

nodes.label: Insert blank page arguments
nodes.body: The chapter writes insert_blank_page(index=2) with the keyword, and the signature of the method is width, height, index in that order (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter writes insert_blank_page(index=2) with the keyword, and the signature of the method is width, height, index in that order (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

A call insert_blank_page(2) made a page 2 points wide, because the first positional argument is the width, and index=2 made a page of the normal 612 points; the writer grew from 6 to 8 pages. The keyword is therefore not a style choice (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: insert_blank_page takes width, height and index in that order, so a single positional number is the width: insert_blank_page(2) made a page 2 points wide, while index=2 made a page of the normal 612 points, and the writer grew from 6 to 8 pages.

nodes.label: Page editing
nodes.body: Page objects are edited in place: rotate() turns a page by a multiple of 90 degrees, clockwise when positive, and merge_page() lays the content of one page on another, a watermark under the text or an overlay over it (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). The chapter rotates every page of the sample chapter in a loop and applies a watermark PDF to pages of it (Sweigart, 2025).

The chapter rotates every page of the sample chapter in a loop and applies a watermark PDF to pages of it (Sweigart, 2025).
One page was rotated by several angles, and a one-word page was merged under and over another, so that the order of the drawing commands shows which is below (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Rotate multiples of90
nodes.body: The chapter rotates pages with the rotate() method of Page objects: 90, 180 or 270 turn the page clockwise and -90, -180 or -270 counterclockwise (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter rotates pages with the rotate() method of Page objects: 90, 180 or 270 turn the page clockwise and -90, -180 or -270 counterclockwise (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

rotate(90) changed the page in place, returned the page object and left the rotation at 90; rotate(45) raised ValueError, Rotation angle must be a multiple of 90. The rotation is stored in the /Rotate entry and the content stream is not changed (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: rotate() takes a multiple of 90, changes the page in place, returns the page and stores the angle (90); rotate(45) raised ValueError, Rotation angle must be a multiple of 90.

nodes.label: Rotation accumulates
nodes.body: Practice question 4 asks how to rotate a page counterclockwise, and the answer in the chapter's own text is a negative angle (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Practice question 4 asks how to rotate a page counterclockwise, and the answer in the chapter's own text is a negative angle (Sweigart, 2025).
Calls add up and the total is not reduced to a turn: 90, 270, -90 and 180 gave 90, 360, 270 and 450. A program that compares rotations must reduce the value modulo 360 itself (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Rotations add up and the sum is not reduced to a turn: rotate(90), rotate(270), rotate(-90) and rotate(180) left the rotations 90, 360, 270 and 450, and a negative angle is stored as given.

nodes.label: Watermark underlay
nodes.body: The chapter merges a one-page watermark PDF into each page with merge_page() and the keyword over=False, so the watermark goes under the text, and notes that the default puts it over (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). Figure 17-3 shows the result (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The chapter merges a one-page watermark PDF into each page with merge_page() and the keyword over=False, so the watermark goes under the text, and notes that the default puts it over (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). Figure 17-3 shows the result (Sweigart, 2025).

A page drawn with BASE and a page with MARK merged with over=False drew MARK before BASE, so the mark is below, and with the default over=True drew BASE and then MARK. On the shipped watermark.pdf the text of page 1 gained blank lines in front of its first line (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: merge_page(watermark, over=False) puts the watermark's drawing commands before the page's own, MARK then BASE, so it lies under the text, and the default over=True puts them after, BASE then MARK.

nodes.label: Merge page in place
nodes.body: The chapter calls page.merge_page(watermark_page, over=False) and then adds the page to the writer, without using a return value (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The chapter calls page.merge_page(watermark_page, over=False) and then adds the page to the writer, without using a return value (Sweigart, 2025).
merge_page() returned None and changed the page it was called on; the text of the merged page was BASEMARK. A program that wants to keep the original page must copy it first (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: merge_page() changes the page it is called on and returns None; the merged page's text came out as BASEMARK.

nodes.label: Protection
nodes.body: PdfWriter.encrypt() accepts a password string and a string that selects the algorithm, and the chapter always uses 'AES-256'; a PdfReader reports is_encrypted and its decrypt() method returns a PasswordType object whose name is NOT_DECRYPTED, USER_PASSWORD or OWNER_PASSWORD (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026). A PDF can have a user password to view it and an owner password to set permissions (Sweigart, 2025).

A PDF can have a user password to view it and an owner password to set permissions (Sweigart, 2025).

Files were written with the default algorithm and with AES-256, opened with the right, wrong and differently capitalised passwords, and written with an empty user password. qpdf and pdftotext confirmed the algorithm and the refusal (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Encrypt rc4 default
nodes.body: The chapter says the encrypt() method accepts a password and a string that selects the algorithm and that it will always use AES-256; the call without an algorithm is not shown (Sweigart, 2025). The pypdf documentation names the algorithms that encrypt() offers (pypdf contributors, 2026).

The pypdf documentation names the algorithms that encrypt() offers (pypdf contributors, 2026).

encrypt('swordfish') without an algorithm wrote RC4 with a 128-bit key: encryption version V 2, revision R 3. qpdf reported R = 3 and no named method. The pypdf installation page says encryption using RC4 is supported by the regular installation and AES needs the crypto extra; the default of the library is the form the chapter never shows (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: encrypt('swordfish') without an algorithm wrote RC4 with a 128-bit key: encryption version V 2, revision R 3, Length 128 and no crypt filter dictionary.

nodes.label: Encrypt aes256
nodes.body: The chapter calls writer.encrypt('swordfish', algorithm='AES-256') and says the argument implements a recommended modern encryption algorithm (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter calls writer.encrypt('swordfish', algorithm='AES-256') and says the argument implements a recommended modern encryption algorithm (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

The file written with AES-256 carried V 5, R 6 and the crypt filter method AESV3, which qpdf reported as AESv3. Two files written from the same writer differed in bytes because of random salts (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: encrypt('swordfish', algorithm='AES-256') wrote V 5, R 6, Length 256 and the crypt filter method /AESV3, which is what the chapter recommends and the only form it shows.

nodes.label: Decrypt return values
nodes.body: The chapter enters is_encrypted, then decrypt('an incorrect password').name, then decrypt('swordfish').name, and explains that decrypt() returns a PasswordType object whose name is NOT_DECRYPTED, USER_PASSWORD or OWNER_PASSWORD (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter enters is_encrypted, then decrypt('an incorrect password').name, then decrypt('swordfish').name, and explains that decrypt() returns a PasswordType object whose name is NOT_DECRYPTED, USER_PASSWORD or OWNER_PASSWORD (Sweigart, 2025)(pypdf contributors, 2026).

nodes.definition: decrypt() returns a PasswordType whose name says which password matched: USER_PASSWORD for userpw, OWNER_PASSWORD for ownerpw and NOT_DECRYPTED for a wrong, empty or differently capitalised password; it raises nothing for a wrong one.

nodes.body: Practice question 3 asks what to do before obtaining Page objects from an encrypted PdfReader, and the answer is to call decrypt() with the password (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Empty user password
nodes.body: The chapter explains that a PDF can have a user password that allows viewing and an owner password that sets permissions for printing, commenting and extracting text (Sweigart, 2025). A reader opens such a file without being given a password.

nodes.label: Word documents
nodes.body: The Word section starts with the Python-Docx package, installed as python-docx and imported as docx, and with the three data types it uses: a Document object for the whole file, Paragraph objects for the paragraphs and Run objects for the stretches of text inside a paragraph (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013). Reading a document means looping over doc.paragraphs and, for a style, setting the style attribute to the name of a paragraph style or a character style (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The Word section starts with the Python-Docx package, installed as python-docx and imported as docx, and with the three data types it uses: a Document object for the whole file, Paragraph objects for the paragraphs and Run objects for the stretches of text inside a paragraph (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013). Reading a document means looping over doc.paragraphs and, for a style, setting the style attribute to the name of a paragraph style or a character style (Sweigart, 2025).

Three ideas carry this subject. The package covers a .docx file as a ZIP archive of XML parts, the body in word/document.xml and the template a new document starts from. Reading text covers paragraphs, runs, and what the paragraphs list leaves out. The style system covers the kinds of style, the names that work and the styles a program can make. Each was run on python-docx 1.2.0 (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Docx package
nodes.body: A Word document has the .docx extension; Python-Docx opens it with docx.Document(filename) and saves with save() (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013). The format is Office Open XML, a ZIP archive of XML parts, which the chapter does not show (Wikipedia, 2026)(Library of Congress, n.d.).

paras.text: A Word document has the .docx extension; Python-Docx opens it with docx.Document(filename) and saves with save() (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013). The format is Office Open XML, a ZIP archive of XML parts, which the chapter does not show (Wikipedia, 2026)(Library of Congress, n.d.).
A new document was saved and opened with zipfile to list its parts and read word/document.xml, and the template that docx.Document() starts from was inspected (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Docx is zip of xml
nodes.body: The chapter says .docx files have many structural elements which Python-Docx represents with three data types, and does not say what a .docx file is on disk (Sweigart, 2025). Office Open XML packages a document as a ZIP archive of XML parts, and a ZIP file usually starts with the bytes PK, the initials of its inventor Phil Katz (Library of Congress, n.d.)(Wikipedia, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says .docx files have many structural elements which Python-Docx represents with three data types, and does not say what a .docx file is on disk (Sweigart, 2025). Office Open XML packages a document as a ZIP archive of XML parts, and a ZIP file usually starts with the bytes PK, the initials of its inventor Phil Katz (Library of Congress, n.d.)(Wikipedia, 2026).

A new document saved by python-docx began with PK and 03 04, held 17 parts including word/document.xml and three relationship files ending in .rels, and could be opened with the zipfile module. The shipped demo.docx has 16 parts (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: A .docx file is a ZIP archive: the first bytes were PK and 03 04, a new document held 17 parts including word/document.xml, and three files ending in .rels tie the parts together.

nodes.label: Document xml body
nodes.body: The paragraphs, runs and text that the chapter names are elements of word/document.xml: w:p for a paragraph, w:r for a run and w:t for the text of a run (Library of Congress, n.d.)(Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The paragraphs, runs and text that the chapter names are elements of word/document.xml: w:p for a paragraph, w:r for a run and w:t for the text of a run (Library of Congress, n.d.)(Canny, 2013).

For add_paragraph('Hello, world!') the body held <w:p><w:r><w:t>Hello, world!</w:t></w:r></w:p>. The structure of the XML is the structure of the three data types: a Document holds paragraphs, a paragraph holds runs (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Default template
nodes.body: The chapter creates a new document with docx.Document() and says the result has no paragraphs (practice question 10) (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation says a new document is created from a default template that the package ships (Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The chapter creates a new document with docx.Document() and says the result has no paragraphs (practice question 10) (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation says a new document is created from a default template that the package ships (Canny, 2013).

The new document had 0 paragraphs, 1 section and more than 100 styles, its core properties named the author python-docx and the year 2013, and the template is the origin of the 164 styles of the next leaves. A file made this way carries those properties unless the program changes them (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: docx.Document() starts from the package's own template and not from an empty file: its author was python-docx, it was created in 2013, it had 0 paragraphs, 1 section and more than 100 styles.

nodes.body: Reading a Word document means opening it with docx.Document(), taking doc.paragraphs, a list of Paragraph objects, and for each paragraph its text and its list of Run objects; a new paragraph begins whenever the user presses ENTER, and a run is a stretch of text with one style (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013). The chapter's get_text() function joins the texts of the paragraphs (Sweigart, 2025).

The chapter's get_text() function joins the texts of the paragraphs (Sweigart, 2025).
A document was built with known runs and read back; a table, a header and a hyperlink were added to show what doc.paragraphs and paragraph.runs leave out (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Paragraphs of body
nodes.body: The chapter's get_text() function and its shell session read doc.paragraphs, a list of Paragraph objects, and join the text attribute of each; practice question 7 asks how to obtain that list (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The chapter's get_text() function and its shell session read doc.paragraphs, a list of Paragraph objects, and join the text attribute of each; practice question 7 asks how to obtain that list (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

The attribute gave a list, in body order, of one, two and an empty string; an empty paragraph counts and so the joined text ends with a newline. The shipped demo.docx has 7 paragraphs and the last one is empty, which the chapter's six printed lines do not show (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: doc.paragraphs is a list of Paragraph objects in body order: the texts were one, two and an empty string (an empty paragraph counts), and joining them with newlines ends with a newline because the last paragraph is empty.

nodes.label: Tables and headers apart
nodes.body: The chapter says a Document object contains a list of Paragraph objects for the paragraphs in the document, and its get_text() function reads only those (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation puts tables in doc.tables and headers in the sections (Canny, 2013).

nodes.label: Hyperlink text and runs
nodes.body: The chapter says a paragraph is a list of runs and that its text attribute is the joined text of them (Sweigart, 2025). A hyperlink in Word is an element of its own that contains runs, and the python-docx documentation describes paragraph.runs as the runs directly in the paragraph (Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The chapter says a paragraph is a list of runs and that its text attribute is the joined text of them (Sweigart, 2025). A hyperlink in Word is an element of its own that contains runs, and the python-docx documentation describes paragraph.runs as the runs directly in the paragraph (Canny, 2013).

A paragraph made of before and a hyperlink containing linked had the text before linked in python-docx 1.2.0, while its runs listed only before. Code that rebuilds a paragraph from its runs loses the link text (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: For a paragraph that contains a hyperlink, text includes the linked words (before linked) in python-docx 1.2.0 but runs lists only 'before ': the linked text is not in any Run, so a program that joins run texts loses it.

nodes.label: Style system
nodes.body: The chapter says Word documents contain three types of styles: paragraph styles apply to Paragraph objects, character styles to Run objects and linked styles to both; to style a paragraph or a run, set its style attribute to the name of the style, and for the linked style of a run add ' Char' to the name (Sweigart, 2025). It prints a list of default style names and says custom styles are made in the Word application (Sweigart, 2025).

It prints a list of default style names and says custom styles are made in the Word application (Sweigart, 2025).

The styles of the template were counted by kind, wrong kinds and wrong names were assigned, the style id the chapter prints was looked up, and a paragraph style was made in code with add_style() (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Style kinds of template
nodes.body: The chapter says Word documents contain three types of styles, paragraph, character and linked, and prints 34 default style names (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation distinguishes paragraph, character, table and numbering (list) styles (Canny, 2013).

The template of a new document has 164 styles: 27 character, 1 list, 36 paragraph and 100 table styles. No kind is called linked; a linked style is a paragraph style with a character style that goes with it, the Quote and Quote Char of the chapter (This study, 2026).

nodes.body: The chapter says to set the style attribute of a Paragraph or Run to the name of the style, and that for a linked style a run uses the name with Char added, paragraphObj.style = 'Quote' and runObj.style = 'Quote Char' (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Word writing
nodes.body: Writing a Word document means calling add_paragraph() and add_run(), add_heading() with a level, add_break() with a break type on a run, and add_picture() with a width and a height, then save(); the chapter shows each in the shell and ends the section with the attributes of a run in Table 17-1 (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013). The document is saved to a .docx file that Word or LibreOffice Writer opens (Sweigart, 2025).

Three ideas carry this subject. Building content covers what add_paragraph(), add_run() and add_heading() return and the heading levels. Run formatting covers the three-valued bold and underline, the attributes that live on run.font and the attribute that is silently ignored. Breaks and pictures covers the page break run, the newline, the size of a picture and the way identical pictures are stored. Each was run on python-docx 1.2.0 (This study, 2026).

Both add_paragraph() and add_run() accept an optional second argument that is a string of the style to use (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Run formatting
nodes.body: Table 17-1 of the chapter lists twelve attributes of a Run object, bold, italic, underline, strike, double_strike, all_caps, small_caps, shadow, outline, rtl, imprint and emboss, and says each can be set to True, False or None, where None makes the run use the style's setting (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation puts the tri-state properties on the font of a run (Canny, 2013).

paras.text: Table 17-1 of the chapter lists twelve attributes of a Run object, bold, italic, underline, strike, double_strike, all_caps, small_caps, shadow, outline, rtl, imprint and emboss, and says each can be set to True, False or None, where None makes the run use the style's setting (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation puts the tri-state properties on the font of a run (Canny, 2013).
Each attribute name was looked up on a Run and on run.font, the XML each value writes was read, and the assignment of an attribute the Run does not have was run (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Tri state bold
nodes.body: The chapter says each text attribute can be set to True, always enabled, False, always disabled, or None, which defaults to whatever the style of the run says (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The chapter says each text attribute can be set to True, always enabled, False, always disabled, or None, which defaults to whatever the style of the run says (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).
A new run's bold was None and wrote nothing. True wrote <w:b/>, False wrote <w:b w:val=0/> and None removed the element again, so the three values are three states of the XML (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Run.bold has three values: None until set (the file says nothing), True writes <w:b/>, False writes <w:b w:val=0/>, and setting None removes the element again.

nodes.label: Underline values
nodes.body: The underline attribute is the one of the three Run attributes that takes more than True and False: the python-docx documentation says it accepts a member of the WD_UNDERLINE enumeration for the kinds of underline (Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The underline attribute is the one of the three Run attributes that takes more than True and False: the python-docx documentation says it accepts a member of the WD_UNDERLINE enumeration for the kinds of underline (Canny, 2013).

True wrote single, WD_UNDERLINE.DOUBLE wrote double and False wrote none in the w:u element. After assigning DOUBLE the attribute read back as the enumeration member and not as True (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: underline takes True (single), a WD_UNDERLINE member such as DOUBLE, or False (none), and writes <w:u w:val=single/>, <w:u w:val=double/> and <w:u w:val=none/>.

nodes.label: Run versus font attributes
nodes.body: Table 17-1 lists twelve attributes under the heading of text attributes that can be set on Run objects: bold, italic, underline, strike, double_strike, all_caps, small_caps, shadow, outline, rtl, imprint and emboss (Sweigart, 2025). Practice question 8 asks what type of object has bold, underline, italic, strike and outline variables (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Table 17-1 lists twelve attributes under the heading of text attributes that can be set on Run objects: bold, italic, underline, strike, double_strike, all_caps, small_caps, shadow, outline, rtl, imprint and emboss (Sweigart, 2025). Practice question 8 asks what type of object has bold, underline, italic, strike and outline variables (Sweigart, 2025).

Looking the names up in python-docx 1.2.0, only bold, italic and underline are attributes of Run, and all twelve are attributes of run.font. The documentation of the Font class lists them (Canny, 2013). The table is correct for the font of a run and wrong for the run Reading the same formatting back is the subject of Runs split at formatting. (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Of the twelve attributes of the chapter's Table 17-1 only bold, italic and underline are attributes of a Run; all twelve, including strike, double_strike, all_caps, small_caps, shadow, outline, rtl, imprint and emboss, are attributes of run.font.

nodes.label: Unknown run attribute ignored
nodes.body: The chapter's sentences about Table 17-1 tell the reader to set the attributes on Run objects, for instance runObj.strike = True (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The chapter's sentences about Table 17-1 tell the reader to set the attributes on Run objects, for instance runObj.strike = True (Sweigart, 2025).

run.strike = True raised no error, and font.strike stayed None with no element in the XML; run.font.strike = True set it and wrote w:strike. A Python object accepts a new attribute without complaint, so the mistake shows only in the output document. All ten interpreters gave the same result (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: run.strike = True raised nothing and changed nothing (font.strike stayed None and the XML had no w:strike element), because Python lets any object take a new attribute; run.font.strike = True set it and wrote the element.

nodes.label: Breaks and pictures
nodes.body: To add a line break rather than a new paragraph the chapter calls add_break() on the Run object after which the break appears, and for a page break passes docx.enum.text.WD_BREAK.PAGE; add_picture() takes a filename and optional width and height, which can be given with docx.shared.Inches() and docx.shared.Cm() (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

Breaks were added and their XML read, a newline and a tab were put in a run, pictures were added with no size, with a width and with both, and three identical pictures were saved and counted in the package (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Page break run
nodes.body: To add a page break the chapter calls add_break() on the Run object after which the break should appear, passing docx.enum.text.WD_BREAK.PAGE, and describes a second page that begins with This is on the second page! (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

paras.text: To add a page break the chapter calls add_break() on the Run object after which the break should appear, passing docx.enum.text.WD_BREAK.PAGE, and describes a second page that begins with This is on the second page! (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

The break is a run holding <w:br w:type=page/>. Both run.add_break(WD_BREAK.PAGE) and add_page_break() wrote one, and add_page_break() added a paragraph of its own. LibreOffice 24.2 counted 2 pages for the file of the chapter and showed both texts (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Newline becomes break
nodes.body: The chapter says that to add a line break rather than a new paragraph one calls add_break() on a run (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation says that a newline or a tab in the text assigned to a run is turned into a break or a tab element (Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The chapter says that to add a line break rather than a new paragraph one calls add_break() on a run (Sweigart, 2025). The python-docx documentation says that a newline or a tab in the text assigned to a run is turned into a break or a tab element (Canny, 2013).

A run with the text a, a tab, b, a newline and c held <w:tab/> and <w:br/> in its XML and gave the same characters back from its text attribute. A newline in the text of a run is therefore a line break, not a new paragraph (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: In the text of a run a tab becomes <w:tab/> and a newline becomes <w:br/>, and reading the run's text gives the tab and the newline back.

nodes.label: Picture size from width
nodes.body: The chapter calls doc.add_picture('zophie.png', width=docx.shared.Inches(1), height=docx.shared.Cm(4)) and says it is easier to give the width and height in inches and centimetres than in the units of the file (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

paras.text: The chapter calls doc.add_picture('zophie.png', width=docx.shared.Inches(1), height=docx.shared.Cm(4)) and says it is easier to give the width and height in inches and centimetres than in the units of the file (Sweigart, 2025)(Canny, 2013).

With neither a size nor resolution recorded the picture took the size of its pixels at 72 per inch; with a width alone the height followed the aspect ratio; with both the picture was stretched to the sizes, so the ratio changed. The shipped zophie.png, 816 by 1088 pixels, gave 0.635 in ratio with Inches(1) and Cm(4) against 0.75 for the image (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: add_picture() with no size uses the size of the image (a 60 by 80 pixel PNG with no resolution recorded came out as 762000 by 1016000 EMU, 72 pixels to the inch), a width alone keeps the aspect ratio (914400 by 1219200) and a width with a height gives both exactly (914400 by 1440000), so the ratio is lost.

nodes.label: Emu units
nodes.body: docx.shared.Inches() and docx.shared.Cm() return lengths, and the python-docx documentation says lengths are integers in English Metric Units, 914,400 to the inch (Canny, 2013).

paras.text: docx.shared.Inches() and docx.shared.Cm() return lengths, and the python-docx documentation says lengths are integers in English Metric Units, 914,400 to the inch (Canny, 2013).

Inches(1) was 914400, Cm(1) was 360000 and Pt(1) was 12700, and Inches(1).inches was 1.0. A width given as a bare integer is read as EMU, so add_picture(width=1) makes a picture about a millionth of an inch wide (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Lengths are integers in English Metric Units: Inches(1) is 914400, Cm(1) is 360000, Pt(1) is 12700, and Inches(1).inches is 1.0.

nodes.label: Picture stored once
nodes.body: Each add_picture() call adds a paragraph with a picture, and the chapter's own session adds one picture (Figure 17-9 shows headings and Figure 17-10 shows the invitation file) (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Practice programs
nodes.body: Project 12 finds all PDF files in the working directory, sorts them alphabetically, copies every page after the first of each to an output PDF and saves it; the three practice programs encrypt and decrypt a folder tree of PDFs, make one invitation per page for each guest, and try the words of a dictionary as a password (Sweigart, 2025).

Each program was written and run on files made for the purpose: the combining with a case-insensitive sort, the walk with a lower-case extension test, the invitations with page breaks, and the dictionary attack on a four-word list. Their results are the leaves below (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Combine all pdfs
nodes.body: Project 12 finds the PDF files of the working directory with os.listdir('.'), sorts them with pdf_filenames.sort(key=str.lower), creates a PdfWriter and, for each file, copies all pages after the first, then saves the output (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Project 12 finds the PDF files of the working directory with os.listdir('.'), sorts them with pdf_filenames.sort(key=str.lower), creates a PdfWriter and, for each file, copies all pages after the first, then saves the output (Sweigart, 2025).

With the name pdf_filenames used in the loop, the three small files gave combined.pdf with A2, B2 and B3, and the one-page file added nothing, as the page range (1, number of pages) is empty for it. A second run would read combined.pdf as input The writer it fills is the empty one of Pdf writer starts empty. (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Project 12 with the loop's list named consistently: three files sorted without regard to case (A_cover, b_report, c_one) and every file's pages from the second on appended gave A2, B2, B3, and the one-page file added nothing.

nodes.label: Case insensitive sort
nodes.body: Step 1 of Project 12 calls the sort() list method on pdf_filenames with the argument key=str.lower, so that the filenames are alphabetized without regard to case (Sweigart, 2025)(Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Step 1 of Project 12 calls the sort() list method on pdf_filenames with the argument key=str.lower, so that the filenames are alphabetized without regard to case (Sweigart, 2025)(Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Sorting Mango.pdf, Zebra.pdf and apple.pdf gave Mango, Zebra, apple without the key and apple, Mango, Zebra with it. The key function only decides the order, and the names keep their case (This study, 2026).

nodes.definition: Sorting puts capital letters first, Mango.pdf, Zebra.pdf, apple.pdf, and key=str.lower, the argument of the chapter's pdf_filenames.sort(), gives apple.pdf, Mango.pdf, Zebra.pdf.

nodes.label: Walk finds all pdfs
nodes.body: PDF Paranoia asks for os.walk() to go through every PDF in a folder and its subfolders, and Project 12 tests filename.endswith('.pdf') (Sweigart, 2025)(Python Software Foundation, 2026).
